title: One model reviews, cheaper models write, a simulation of 1600 careers decides what ships. My AI pipeline for a racing career sim
author: UnEagle
selftext:
Solo, 8 weeks, 1000+ commits, no hand-written code. Racing Driver Simulator is a text-based racing career sim (karting at 8, budget, sponsors, contracts, six tiers up to the top). The video is one season on desktop, including a special race.



Three things that actually kept the AI from breaking the game:



1. The expensive model never writes code. It writes the spec and reviews the diff. A cheaper model gets the spec and nothing else: no chat history, no notes. Scope drift stopped the day I did this.



2. A shell script checks every diff before any model looks at it: files in scope, clean index, tests actually run. Zero tokens. It catches most of what my review comments used to be about.



3. The sim judges the sim. Every release runs 1600 simulated careers against fixed thresholds (dynasty rate, bankruptcy per tier, how often a wonderkid reaches F1) and a golden-seed replay that must match bit for bit. Green unit tests still let the same team win 9 titles in a row. The gate doesn't.



Cost: a mid-size feature is $5 to $10 for the coder, bigger rewrites around $100, the reviewer is 15 to 20% of spend. Two releases a week.



AI disclosure: code and minimal art are AI-made under my direction; design, rules, economy and the thresholds are mine.



Play it: [https://racingdriversim.com](https://racingdriversim.com) (free, browser, no account). Curious how others gate AI-written game logic. Statistical gates, or all playtesting?

comments.author: GridIron-Grit
comments.body:
Somethings for SIM quality I learned:

Run the simulations daily. Like take entire dev arc just to ensure the probes/measurements/output are all well understood as you do feature Arcs then automate it running on your idle box. keep the results.   
  
[Gridiron\_Grit](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4887480/Gridiron_Grit/) keeps NFL stat accuracy 30years team, careers come and go without ever seeing a 5k rushing yards season.

I'll check your game out!

replies.author: UnEagle
replies.body:
Thanks, that's a good push. Right now the full pass runs per release (35 to 50 min on the VPS), plus smaller probes during a feature arc, and every run is kept as a snapshot next to a frozen baseline so I can see drift between releases, not just pass/fail. Daily on the idle box is the obvious next step and basically free, so I'll wire it up.

How do you set the bounds in Gridiron\_Grit? Mine are hand-picked thresholds (no team wins more than X titles in a row, bankruptcy per tier within a window). Do you fit them to the real-world distribution, or also hand-tune? The "no 5k rushing season in 30 years" kind of check is exactly the thing I'd like more of.

comments.author: Spare-Mammoth-6652
comments.body: What player policies drive the 1,600 careers: random choices, fixed strategies, or something adaptive? Comparing the balance metrics separately for conservative, aggressive and exploit-seeking strategies could be useful alongside the golden replay. An acceptable overall bankruptcy rate could still hide one strategy that almost always fails or dominates.

replies.author: UnEagle
replies.body:
Fixed strategies, not adaptive. The balance pass uses four archetypes: ambitious (always takes the step up), cautious (prefers to stay), vagabond (parallel and alternative series) and budget (buys promotions), crossed with four career starts and difficulty levels, so each cell gets every strategy. That crossing exists because of a review finding: an earlier version tied start and strategy to the same counter, so each start had exactly one strategy and the ceilings were measured on a population that didn't exist. Decoupling them moved the thresholds.

Title ceilings (max titles in a row, max titles in a career) are gated by a separate "chase titles" policy that always takes the best seat, because the averaged archetypes never touch the ceiling and the old assertion there was blind for weeks before I noticed.

Your point about one strategy hiding inside an acceptable average is fair. Per start and difficulty I already gate separately; per archetype I only report counts, not thresholds. That's a gap. The event layer has a separate harness with 8 bots including explicit exploit seekers (farm bad luck for compensation, promise and break it) with pass/fail on exploits, so that part is covered, but the core economy isn't gated per strategy yet. Adding it.
